title: Accounts, Dopharm, and Security

lessons.title: Account Types and What to Do With Them

teach.title: Why Do People Buy Accounts?
teach.body:
In M02, we already discussed that it’s best to protect your own personal account [→ Lesson 2.1]. In M03, we mentioned that people buy pre-made accounts [→ Lesson 3.2]. Now let’s break down the complete classification and when to use each type.

People buy accounts because:
- A new, self-registered account has minimal trust and very low limits
- Facebook is suspicious of accounts that start running ads immediately after registration
- Purchased, pre-set up accounts already have some activity and a higher starting trust score

teach.title: Autoreg (Autoregistration)
teach.body:
An account created automatically or manually with no real activity. Minimal trust. Doesn’t last long with aggressive advertising.

Typical auto-registered account: a newly registered profile with no friends, no posts, and a new email address. Facebook detects an “empty” account and treats it with suspicion.

Where to use: testing new hypotheses where it’s okay to lose an account quickly. As a “warm reserve”—purchased in dozens for rapid rotation.

Price: $0.35–1.5 depending on the GEO. UA is the cheapest ($0.35–0.87). USA is the most expensive.

teach.title: A farm account
teach.body:
An account that has undergone manual or semi-automatic setup: friends have been added (either fake or real accounts), there is organic activity, a Fan Page is present, and several weeks of "live" behavior.

The standard for most arbitrageurs. A balance between price and trust.

Price: $2–10 depending on GEO, farm quality, and duration.

teach.title: King (Aged/Old Account)
teach.body:
The account was registered 1–5+ years ago. It may have real or organically simulated activity during this time. Higher initial trust score, higher initial limits.

Used for scaling when a stable foundation is needed or for high-cost GEOs where reliability is important.

Price: $12–26+ depending on the GEO and quality.

teach.title: PZRD (Passed the advertising defense test)
teach.body:
An account that has previously been restricted from advertising and has successfully passed Facebook’s review (“rehabilitated”). Facebook has already reviewed this account and confirmed that it is genuine. This increases the initial trust score.

Abbreviation: PZRD — "Passed advertising review." The abbreviation ZRD is also used in the community.

Price: $4–25+ depending on the GEO. U.S.: $28–50+.

teach.title: Agency Accounts and BM Rentals
teach.body:
Instead of buying regular accounts, rent access to whitelisted advertising accounts from Meta Business Partners. Highest trust, minimal bans, and high-quality support.

Price: 1.5–10% of ad spend + setup fee ($20–100) + often a minimum top-up ($200–500).

Not recommended for beginners due to the cost. Best used when scaling up to $500–1,000 per day.

Details — [→ Library: Agency Accounts]

teach.title: What to Choose at the Start
teach.body:
**First Test:** A farm account targeting the desired GEO ($2–10). Optimal balance between price and trust.

**Scaling:** Add King or PZRD accounts for more stable results.

**Aggressive verticals (nutra, gambling):** Consider King or agency accounts from the start.

pairs: Created with friends and enthusiasm, the Media Buyer Standard
An old account (1–5+ years old), with a higher starting trust
Passed Facebook's review following the restrictions

teach.title: What is Dopharm and what is it used for?
teach.body:
**Dofarm** isn’t about building an account from scratch. It’s about preparing an account you’ve already purchased to run ads. The goal: to minimize suspicious activity and let Facebook see a “real” person before the first ad campaign launches.

When you buy an account and log in, Facebook detects a change in device, IP address, and possibly location. If you launch ads immediately afterward, it’s a suspicious signal. The risk of verification or a ban increases dramatically.

“Dofarm” refers to a few days of organic activity, after which the account will be “warmed up” for advertising.

teach.title: Step-by-Step Guide to Dofarm
teach.body:
**Day 1 — First Login:**
- Load your profile in an anti-detection browser with the correct GEO proxy
- 15–20 minutes of organic activity: scroll through your feed, like posts, leave a few neutral comments
- Visit 1–2 external sites (Google, a news portal) — this mimics real user behavior
- Check your account settings: language, time zone, contacts
- DO NOT log into Business Manager and DO NOT touch any advertising tools
- Log out. Do not log in again today

**Day 2 — Preparing the Fan Page:**
- Use the same profile and proxy (always the same one)
- 15–20 minutes of activity in the News Feed
- Create a Fan Page based on the offer’s theme (or a broad topic: health, lifestyle)
- Fill out the Fan Page as completely as possible: profile picture, cover photo, description, address (can be fictional), phone number, hours of operation, category
- Make 2–3 posts on the Fan Page (can be reposts from other pages or neutral content)
- DO NOT access Business Manager or advertising tools

**Days 3–4 — Warming Up the Fan Page:**
- Continue posting to the feed
- Add another 3–5 posts to the Fan Page
- If possible, boost the page’s follower count by 100–200 [→ Resource Library: Follower Boost]
- Run a small ad campaign for the post targeting “Engagement” ($2–3)—this sends the first positive signal to Facebook
- The last post before launching the main ad campaign—preferably the exact creative you’ll be promoting. Facebook will already have reviewed the text and images before the main launch

**Day 5+ — Launch the ad campaign:**
- Connect your Business Manager and ad account
- Link a credit card
- Start with a small budget ($5–15/day)
- Don’t jump straight to the maximum

teach.title: Critical Rules for Dofarm
teach.body:
**Always use the same profile and proxy.** Never change the proxy for your account during or after the farm. Changing your IP = a red flag.

**Never log in from a real device.** If you created an account on a phone without anti-detection software, Facebook has detected a new device. Risk of verification or a ban.

**Your behavior should look human.** Don’t log in and log out immediately. Scroll through your feed, linger on content, like various posts, and occasionally write comments.

**Account GEO = proxy GEO.** If it’s a Polish account, log in via a Polish proxy. Always.

items: First entry: organic engagement without ads
Creating and Filling Out a Fan Page
Launch of the main advertising campaign

lessons.title: Why Users Get Banned and How to Avoid It

teach.title: Main Reasons for Bans
teach.body:
**1. Violations of Advertising Policies**
Prohibited content in creatives or text: medical guarantees (“will cure,” “guaranteed”), negative references to personal characteristics, shocking or manipulative content. Facebook scans automatically and performs manual reviews.

**2. Suspicious Logins**
Changes in IP address or device, or unusual geographic location. This is why anti-detection measures and a stable proxy are critically important.

**3. Low account trust**
A new account with no activity, rejected credit cards, and many rejected ads—all of these lower trust and increase the risk of a ban.

**4. Mass complaints from the audience**
If people are clicking “Hide Ad” or “Report” en masse, Facebook gets a signal that the ad is irrelevant or annoying. High frequency combined with weak creative → complaints → account issues.

**5. Payment Issues**
Rejected cards, suspicious payment patterns. Failed chargebacks are a serious blow to trust.

**6. Linked Blocked Accounts**
If Facebook links an account to one that’s already been banned (due to a shared IP, card, Business Manager, or Fan Page)—the ban can be imposed automatically. That’s exactly why isolating accounts using anti-detection measures and separate proxies is so important.

teach.title: How to Minimize Risks
teach.body:
- A stable anti-detection and proxy profile for each account
- High-quality pre-launch setup
- Creatives without obvious violations (or cloaking for gray-market offers)
- A separate account for each account
- Frequency monitoring—if the frequency rises above 3–4, update the creatives or audience
- Backup accounts are always ready

l1.q: Facebook blocked the ad. Text: "Are you suffering from pain? Our cream will completely cure you in 10 days!" What violates the rules?
options: "You're Suffering" — A Reflection on Pain
"Will completely cure" — a guaranteed medical claim is prohibited
"10 days" — a specific timeframe is a manipulation
"Our Cream" — You Can't Advertise Someone Else's Product

l1.q: Frequency 6.2. What does this mean, and what does it do?
options: Great—the audience will remember it
The audience is oversaturated—there's a risk of complaints and a drop in CTR; it's time to update your creatives or expand your audience
Frequency does not affect bans
Increase the budget to reach new people

lessons.title: Types of Bans and What to Do Afterward

teach.title: Hierarchy of Restrictions
teach.body:
**Ad rejection** — the least severe situation. A specific ad did not pass moderation. The campaign and account are active.
Action: Edit the creative or text and resubmit for review. Or file an appeal if you believe it was a mistake.

**Ad Account Restriction** — The ad account has been restricted. The Business Manager and personal account are still active.
Action: File an appeal via the support form. While you wait, run campaigns from a backup account. The restriction is often lifted after a successful appeal.

**Business Manager Ban** — The BM is blocked, as are all accounts within it.
Action: The appeal process is more complicated. If unsuccessful—create a new BM using a different personal account.

**Personal account ban**—the most serious situation. It can affect the BM and all accounts.
Action: File an appeal, but success is not guaranteed.

teach.title: A Proper Appeal
teach.body:
- Fill out the form as thoroughly and politely as possible
- Explain what happened and why you believe the restriction is incorrect
- Provide specific details: which ads, the reason for the rejection
- DO NOT write in an aggressive or demanding tone—it reduces your chances
- Wait 24–72 hours
- If unsuccessful, try again with different wording
- If the appeal is unsuccessful, switch to a new account

teach.title: Rules After a Ban
teach.body:
**Never try to bypass a ban from the same device and IP address without anti-detection measures and a new proxy.** Facebook will identify you, and your next account will also get banned.

**Working in parallel:** If your advertising account gets banned, launch a backup account immediately. Don’t wait for the appeal result.

l1.q: Match the type of constraint with the correct response:
pairs: Appeal + backup account while you wait
An appeal or a new BM using a different account

teach.title: The Principle of Diversification
teach.body:
If you have just one account and it gets banned, your work comes to a complete halt for several days. If you have a structured setup, the ban on a single account is just a technical issue that can be resolved in 30 minutes.

**Basic structure for a solo media buyer:**

- **Main account** — where profitable campaigns run
- **Backup account × 1–2** — ready to launch, fully set up, with a linked card. If the main account gets banned, you switch to this one immediately
- **Test account** — for initial testing of new connections so as not to risk the main account

teach.title: Isolation Rules in the Account Park
teach.body:
- Each account is a separate profile in the anti-detection browser
- Each account has its own proxy
- Each account has its own card
- Never share Fan Pages between accounts
- Keep backup accounts fully farm-ready—do not start farming after a ban

teach.title: Why the reserve must be prepared in advance
teach.body:
Dofarm takes 4–5 days. If you start after a ban, that’s 4–5 days of downtime. At $100/day in profit, that’s $400–500 lost.

A ready-to-use backup account = zero downtime in the event of a ban.

Rule: Buy new accounts in advance, not after you’ve been banned. When scaling up, always keep 2–3 backup accounts ready.

teach.title: Teamwork
teach.body: When working as a team, each media buyer has their own isolated set of accounts. Never allow two people to access the same account at the same time—Facebook detects different devices and IP addresses, which raises a red flag.

lessons.title: Cloaking: Why It's Used and How It Works

teach.title: The Mechanics of Cloaking
teach.body:
In M03, we learned about cloaking [→ Lesson 3.4]. Now let’s take a closer look at how it works.

**Principle:** The tracker (usually Keitaro) analyzes each incoming request and decides what to display:
- Facebook moderator or bot → “blank page” (harmless content)
- Real user → real offer

**How a moderator is identified:**
- IP addresses of Facebook servers and known verification services (constantly updated databases)
- Browser user-agent (known crawlers and bots)
- Behavioral patterns: immediate transition without delay, no scrolling, specific viewport dimensions
- Time between the click and the page opening

Cloaking must be constantly maintained—databases of moderators’ IP addresses are updated, and outdated cloaking ceases to filter effectively.

teach.title: When to Use Cloaking and When Not to
teach.body:
**Required:**
- Nutra offers with direct medical claims (Facebook blocks them)
- Gambling and betting (prohibited in most GEOs)
- Any ad where the actual content will not pass moderation

**NOT needed:**
- Product ads — most simple products pass moderation without cloaking
- White-hat offers (finance, e-commerce, education)
- Anything where you can write copy that will pass moderation

**For beginners:** Start without cloaking. Test creatives that comply with Facebook’s rules. Learn about cloaking once you move on to gray-area verticals with real-world experience.

teach.title: Risks of Cloaking
teach.body:
- Direct violation of Facebook's rules
- If detected, the account and Business Manager will be banned, and all associated accounts will often be banned as well
- Requires constant maintenance of cloaking databases
- Additional costs and complexity

l1.q: A media buyer is promoting a pain relief cream (product). The ad is passing moderation without any issues. Is cloaking necessary?
options: Yes—it always improves results
No—if an offer passes moderation without cloaking, then it's unnecessary and only adds to the complexity.
Depends on GEO
That's right—without cloaking, Facebook shows ads to moderators

l1.q: How does the tracker identify a Facebook moderator?
options: Based on the amount of money on the card
Based on IP address, user-agent, and behavioral patterns
By the number of friends on Facebook
By Internet speed

summary:
After completing this module, the student will:

- Know the different types of accounts and when to use each one
- Be able to properly farm a purchased account within 4–5 days
- Know the main reasons for bans and how to minimize them
- Understand the different types of restrictions and the correct response to each
- Be able to build a basic account portfolio
- Understand cloaking, when it’s necessary, and when there are simpler solutions

**Next module:** Career and the independent buyer.
